claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations feature lets component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself by translating the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi determines which resources need to change.
With Pulumi's component state migrations feature, component authors can change a component's internal design and include the migration in the same release.
The Pulumi state migrations API is experimental and may change.
Pulumi hosts a component state migrations discussion at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799 where feedback can be shared.
The legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the AWSX VPC example, a security group sits outside the `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component and refers to the VPC.
Without a state migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading a component could replace the VPC instead of preserving it.
Per the AWS CloudFormation documentation, an EC2 SecurityGroup resource must be replaced if its VpcId property changes.
The modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component can be upgraded to from the legacy AWSX VPC component while keeping the existing network intact.
The third version of the example removes AWSX and declares the VPC resources directly using the `@pulumi/aws` provider package.
Across all three versions of the AWSX VPC example, the underlying AWS resource IDs stay the same even though how Pulumi records the resources and their relationships changes.

In v1 of the AWSX VPC example, the component tree is rooted at `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing an `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc`, an `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet "vpc-isolated-0"` (itself containing a subnet, route table, and route table association), and an `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway "vpc"` containing an internet gateway.

In v2 of the AWSX VPC example, the component tree is rooted at `awsx:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing an `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc`, which directly contains the subnet (`vpc-isolated-1`), route table, route table association, and internet gateway without wrapper components.

In v3 of the AWSX VPC example, the resource tree is rooted directly at `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"` with no `awsx:` component wrappers, containing the subnet, route table, route table association, and internet gateway.
In Pulumi's state, each record — whether a physical resource or a component grouping resources — has a Pulumi name called a URN.
Managed resources in Pulumi state have an ID from the cloud provider, such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate wrapper components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the AWSX VPC example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` in the legacy version to `vpc-isolated-1` in the modern version.
Pulumi resource aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
In the example, a new VPC component is registered with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback passed through a `stateMigrations` option.
The `migrateClassicVpc` function comes from the example's migration file at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
A state-migration alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the migration callback then receives the old component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A Pulumi component state migration callback returns a `newState` value containing the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children, and a `successors` value mapping each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.
The full migration code for the first migration in the example is available at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
In the example's migration callback, the first checks make the callback safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, the callback does nothing.
In the example's migration callback, an unexpected component type raises an error instead of attempting to guess how to migrate it.
The example's `rename` helper copies a saved state record and changes its URN, type, and parent while preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.
In the first migration, the `rename` helper moves the subnet record to be under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in the migration's `successors` map let the Pulumi engine know that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet both point to the same new subnet record.
Pulumi uses the `successors` mappings from a state migration to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.

In the example, the security group lives outside the VPC component, and the VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference to the VPC connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The third version of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws` instead of using an AWSX component.
The second migration in the example removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place, so that both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record.
In the second migration, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it in the resource tree.
In the example's third version, the VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs component state-migration callbacks in order, passing each callback's result to the next callback.
In the example, a stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version by running both migration callbacks in sequence.
In the example, a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration callback.
In the example, once both migrations have run, both migration callbacks return no result on later updates.
After a Pulumi component state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In the example, keeping resource IDs does not guarantee an empty preview: the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.

Running `pulumi preview` before each upgrade in the example should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
Pulumi's `pulumi preview` command evaluates a component state migration without saving it, while `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.
When a component registers a state migration inside its implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state themselves.
When users upgrade a component with a registered state migration and run Pulumi, Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
The component state migrations guide at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covers the callback contract.
The VPC example at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration contains all three programs and the migration code shown in the post.
Pulumi's documentation on component state migrations is located at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/.
An AWSX VPC migration example is hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration.
State migration callbacks run during Pulumi previews and updates when prior state exists.
State migration callbacks must be idempotent.
State migration callbacks return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.

A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings, where each mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result if no migration is needed.

The Pulumi state entries used in component state migrations follow the checkpoint resource format described at https://pulumi-developer-docs.readthedocs.io/latest/docs/references/deployment-schema.html#pulumi-resource-state, including fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
The Pulumi option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the state migration callback API.
A Pulumi component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results in Pulumi component state migrations do not require removing an already-applied migration.
